title: Being Unique

paragraphs.text: As a biologist, and, obviously, as a human being, I often ask Who am I? The question seems simple, yet without an answer we lack the inner compass that guides us through life. Self-analysis may offer partial insight into this vital question. A fuller understanding of self, however, emerges from our social interactions within our environment. One interesting aspect of identity is a person’s drive to be different and special. In recent decades, psychologists have defined this facet of personality as the need for uniqueness, with research revealing that everyone tries hard to create uniqueness to some degree. More surprising, perhaps, is that we try to set ourselves apart by affiliating with those people in society who are ‘more like us’, creating a combination of alliances. Moreover, the drive to be unique has broad effects: in terms of appearance, clothing is the obvious example, though nowadays in some countries many people choose tattoos as fashion or cultural statements. Uniqueness is also an important driver of discoveries. Albert Einstein produced little under the constraints of academia, but achieved greater success independently. And if scientist Marie Curie had conformed to the social expectations for her gender, the world would have been deprived of her many contributions.

The idea of a need for uniqueness originated with the study of its counterpart, conformity. In the 1950s, psychologist Solomon Asch set up an experiment in which a participant sat with several other people who had secretly been hired by Asch. The task was to look at a line drawn on paper and then pick which one of three other lines most closely resembled the initial prompt. Identifying the proper line should have been simple. But the hired actors responded before the real participant, and all gave the same wrong answer. When the participants’ turn came, about a third responded just as the actors did - an astonishing fraction, given that the correct choice was clear. Although the participants had initially arrived at the proper response, they began doubting themselves and concluded the group was right.

In the 1970s, psychologists Howard L. Fromkin and Charles R. Snyder devised a uniqueness scale. They discovered that relatively simple questions can gauge the intensity of this need. In it, respondents rate how strongly certain statements apply to them, such as ‘I express my opinions openly’ and ‘I live according to the standards of society.’ Using this scale for one of my own experiments, I looked at how the need for uniqueness related to the basic human characteristics recognized by most psychologists: extroversion, openness to experience, agreeableness, conscientiousness and neuroticism. In a survey of 150 students, I found the first three traits are closely connected with the need for uniqueness.

Although a person’s need to seek uniqueness is generally stable throughout life, certain situations can shift it temporarily. In 2009 I assisted in a study conducted by psychologist Roland Imhoff, who wanted to investigate how making someone feel average might affect subsequent behavior. To do so, we asked subjects to complete a personality test. We then gave them inaccurate information about how they performed in the test; half the participants were told they had very pronounced individual traits, the other half informed that their personality was simply normal.

Next we asked how they felt about a current debate regarding dining cars on trains and said we had conducted a survey. To test whether the personality test results altered their desire to stand out, we showed two charts, claiming that either 79% or 21% of the survey respondents believed that dining cars should be dropped. Interestingly, the subjects who had been told they were average were far likelier to opt for the minority opinion. In contrast, those that were told they had unique traits tended to agree with the majority. We interpreted this as meaning that the people led to believe they were unremarkable offered an opposing opinion to differentiate themselves. People will express their individuality even in something as mundane as dining cars.

In 1999, psychologists Heejung Kim and Hazel Rose Markus recruited North Americans and East Asians waiting at San Francisco International Airport for an interesting experiment. To disguise the true purpose of the study, the participants were asked to fill out a survey in exchange for a free pen. On completion, the experimenter reached into a bag and pulled out four green pens and one orange pen. Which color a person selected was the real test. North Americans opted for the rarer choice three times out of four, whereas only one in four East Asians chose the less common color. Kim and Markus then analyzed 300 advertisements, finding that Korean advertisements were highly likely to highlight conformity, and US advertisers more commonly underscored how products make someone stand out.

This leads us on to the concept of individualism versus collectivism. Individualist cultures such as the UK and the Netherlands emphasize the right of individuals to think and behave independently without social restriction. Collectivism, however, values co-operation - the members of a group striving towards something that benefits them all. In 2010 economist Yuriy Gorodnichenko compared data across countries, and found strong positive correlations between a country’s individualism and its measures of innovation in science and technology. He also claimed that increasing individualism within a country meant that the level of wealth and comfort per person became higher. However, it is important to remember that humans evolved as a group-living species: the division of food and other vital supplies and the division of labor are the advantages of belonging to a group.

highlight the role that authority figures play in shaping people’s choices.

options.text: measure and evaluate the level of the need for uniqueness in individuals.
